options: Well-formed: `f(double)` is private, so `f(int)` is called after converting `1.0`
Ill-formed: overload resolution selects the private `f(double)`
Ill-formed: the call is ambiguous between the two overloads
Undefined behavior: a private member function is called from outside the class
questions.explanation: Access is checked after overload resolution. `f(double)` is an exact match and wins; then the compiler finds it is private in this context and the program is ill-formed. Access never removes a candidate, so the first option, which is what many people expect, describes a rule C++ does not have. There is no ambiguity because the exact match beats the floating-integral conversion.

options: Neither: `C` inherits `B`'s friendship
Only `B::f`, because a friend class must be declared before `A`
Both, because `secret` is private
Only `C::g`
questions.explanation: Friendship is not inherited: `A` granted access to `B`, and a class derived from `B` gets none of it, so `C::g` is ill-formed. `B::f` is fine because `B`'s member functions have the same access as `A`'s own members, and a friend declaration may name a class that is declared later. The tempting first option treats friendship like a member that a derived class inherits, which it is not.

options: `B`, because `D::f` is private and cannot be called
Nothing: the program is ill-formed because an override may not be less accessible
Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: Access for a virtual call is checked on the name in the call expression, using the static type: `b.f()` names `B::f`, which is public. The call then dispatches to the final overrider, `D::f`, and prints `D`. An override may have any access; only `d.f()` would be ill-formed. Access never changes which function a virtual call reaches.

questions.prompt: Which member function of `Derived` is ill-formed?
options: Only `c`
Only `b`, because `d` might be a different object
`b` and `c`, since both access another object's protected member
None of them
questions.explanation: A protected non-static member of `Base` may be used in `Derived` only through an object expression of type `Derived` or a class derived from it. `a` uses `this->x` and `b` uses a `Derived&`, so both are fine, even though `d` is another object. `c` goes through a plain `Base&`, which might be a sibling class's object, so the extra protected check makes it ill-formed.

options: Well-formed: `A` is a public namespace-scope struct
Ill-formed: a class cannot use a type that its base inherits privately
Ill-formed: `A` finds the injected-class-name inherited through `B`, which is private
Well-formed, but `a` has type `B::A`, a distinct type
questions.explanation: Every class has its own name injected into its scope as a member. Unqualified lookup inside `C` searches `C`'s bases before the namespace, so `A` finds `A`'s injected-class-name as a member of `B`, where it is private because `B` inherits `A` privately. Writing `::A a;` finds the namespace-scope name and is well-formed, which shows the second option is wrong: the type itself is usable, only that spelling is not.

options: Only #1
Both: `show` is a member of namespace `n`
Only #2
Neither: a friend defined in a class is a member function of that class
questions.explanation: A friend function first declared in a class is a member of the enclosing namespace, but it is not visible to ordinary or qualified lookup; only argument-dependent lookup finds it, through the associated class `V`. So #1 works and #2 is ill-formed. The second option is half right: `show` really does belong to `n`, it just cannot be named that way until it is also declared at namespace scope.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what does this program do?
options: Ill-formed: `&Vault::gold` names a private member
Undefined behavior: private members may not be read from outside
Ill-formed: a friend function cannot be defined in a class template
It prints `7`
questions.explanation: The usual access checking rules do not apply to names in the declaration of an explicit instantiation, so `&Vault::gold` is allowed as a template argument there. Instantiating `Thief` defines the friend `steal`, which returns that pointer to member, and `v.*steal()` reads `gold`. The first option would be right for an ordinary use such as `Thief<&Vault::gold> t;`. Access is a compile-time rule about names, so nothing here is undefined.

options: Only `Inner::get`: a nested class has no special access to its enclosing class
Only `Outer::peek`
Both
Neither: enclosing and nested classes are implicitly friends of each other
questions.explanation: A nested class is a member of its enclosing class and, since C++11 (CWG 45), has the same access as any other member, so `Inner::get` may read `Outer::x`. The relationship is one-way: [class.access.nest] gives the enclosing class no special access to the nested class's members, so `peek` cannot read `Inner::y` and is ill-formed. The first option describes the C++98 wording, which compilers no longer follow.
